title: The Cholas and their Coinage
author: T. Desikachariar
text: THE CHOLAS AND THEIR COINAGE BY DIWAN BAHADUR T. DESIKACHARI, B.A., B.L., M.R.A.S. CENTURIES before the Christian era, the Cholas had established themselves on the coast of Coromandel (Chola mandalam) and enjoyed a civilization not less advanced than that of the Aryan Settlements in the North. They were referred to along with the Keralas and the Pandyas in the Second Rock Edict of the Buddhist Emperor, Asoka, in the third century B.C. The great chronicle of Ceylon, an ancient work in Pali called the Mahavanso, made it the theme of one of its main episodes, the war waged against the Island by the Chola Tamils in the early centuries preceding the Christian era. Some scholars have advanced the hypothesis that it was a colony of Dravidian merchants who, becoming acquainted with an alphabetic writing derived from the white Pre-Semetic Akkadians north of the Euphrates Valley, brought the script to India, being thus the first to introduce the art of writing into Dravida Desam. There is in the proof that is adduced in support of this hypothesis much that tends to show that the Tamils, as early as the seventh century before the Christian era, had developed such a degree of maritime and commercial enterprise as to tempt them to undertake voyages across the sea to distant countries. The principal port of the Cholas was Kaveripaddinam, situated near the northern mouth of the Kaveri. The first capital of the Cholas was Uraiyur. probably the oldest portion of the modern Trichinopoly ; and later on they ruled from their capital Jayam-Koṇda-Cholapuram, in the Udaiyarpalayam Taluq of the Trichinopoly District, the relics of whose greatness are still to be seen in an embankment, many miles long, of a ruined reservoir, probably one of the largest in India, and a temple which, even in its present neglected condition, attests to its once magnificent proportions and costly Dravidian architecture. Other places there are too in the same District, which remind us by their names of these ancient rulers, such as Gangai-Koṇda-Cholapuram and Gandarādittam. As the Chola kings grew in power they had their capitals Tanjore, Kumbakonam and Conjivaram and their Viceroys in Rajahmundry in the north and Madura in the South. It is interesting to note that when Samudragupta raided the South about 340 A.D., a Pallava ruled at Kanchi. In addition to the notice of their existence in the Asoka Edicts and the Mahavanso, before the Christian era, we find allusions to the Cholas, in the Periplus Maris Erithræ in the first century, in Ptolemy's Geography in the second century, in the travels of Hiun Thsang in the seventh century and in the travels of Marco Polo in the thirteenth century of the Christian era. Beyond references to the existence of the Cholas as a ruling power there is nothing in these contemporary records that could help us in the construction of a connected Chola History. Nor do we derive substantial aid from Sanskrit or Tamil writings, which give conflicting accounts the accuracy of which has yet to be confirmed by lithic records which however have so far not taken us earlier than the eighth century A.D. We, no doubt, now and then meet with in the indigenous literature names like Köchengannán and Karikâla. Of these, the latter is reputed to have built the Kaveri embankments, employed forced labour paying them with leather money, thus invoking the anger of the Gods and a dust-storm which destroyed his capital, and probably ruled in the second century of the Christian era. The same name is also mentioned as that of the persecutor of the great Vaishnavite Reformer, Ramanujacharya, who had to flee out of the Chola kingdom and take refuge with the King Vishnu Vardhana. But all these sovereigns have yet to be allotted their proper places in Chola genealogy. The Chola inscriptions and coins which have hitherto come to light relate to a period between the ninth and thirteenth centuries of the Christian era, during which the Cholas rose into great prominence and finally declined, leaving only the numerous South Indian Temples, inscriptions and coins to attest to their greatness. Inscriptions are, however, not wanting to show that the Cholas were a power to be reckoned with even anterior to the eighth century of the Christian era. During the supremacy of that strange race, the Pallavas, the Cholas seem to have occupied but a subordinate position, but had never lost their native virility or a good portion of their inherited dominions. It is when the history of the Pandyan kings becomes intimately connected with that of the Chola and Sinhalese sovereigns that we begin to have the help of Epigraphy and Numismatics. It is then too that the account in the Mahavanso of the inroads of the Tamils into the island of Ceylon and of the reprisals of the Sinhalese on the mainland come to be matter of lithic record. Between the ninth and thirteenth centuries of the Christian era the Chola kings, with varying success, attempted to maintain their supremacy over the whole of the Southern Presidency. In order to understand the coins of this period, it is necessary to bear in mind who were the contemporary kings that ruled in different portions of the country over which the Cholas struggled for predominence. There were the Chalukyas of Rajahmundry in the north and the Pallavas who had ruled on the Coromandel coast with Kanchipuram as their capital. From Nellore and the Ghauts to the sea, was the ancient Dravida Desam, or the land of the Tamils, of which the northern portion the Chola Desam, extended from the Kaveri to the Palar; from the Kaveri to Comorin was the Pandya country; and the Chera country comprised all the territory westward as far as the sea. Another race of kings playing a prominent part in the Chola history of this period are the Gangas, who ruled probably from Mukkalingam near Parlakimedi in the Ganjam District. And if to these be added the Sinhalese sovereigns who governed the Island of Ceylon, during the time of the Chola ascendancy in the mainland and the King of Pegu, the tale of sovereignties, with the conquest of which the Chola history mainly deals, would be almost complete. A fairly reliable genealogy of the Chola soveriegns of this period is now available. Parantaka ruled from A.D. 907 to 949, from Uraiyur and was known as 'Madurantaka' and 'Vira Narayana.' The Jains were numerically strong during his reign but he is also reputed to have built the Kanaka Sabha or the Golden Hall of the Chidambaram Temple, a meritorious act of devotion to Siva, to which more than one Chola sovereign lays claim. No coins of the king have been yet found. After Parantaka (whose accession was in A.D. 907 and death in A.D. 949) till we come to the time of his great grandson Raja Raja, who ascended the throne in A.D. 985, we meet with the name of no remarkable Chola king. 'Certain inscriptions of Parantaka are of special interest to the student of village institutions by reason of the full details they give of the manner in which local affairs were administered by well organised local committees, or Panchayats exercising administrative and judicial control under royal sanction.' The immediate predecessor of Raja Raja, was the grandson of Parantaka and the son of Gandaraditya. He assumed the title of Madurantaka and was known as Uttama Chola. To this monarch must be assigned, one of the two varieties of coins, bearing the legend 'Uttama Chola' in Grandha characters, and having a seated tiger with a fish. in front of it, the tiger being the dynastic emblem of the Cholas and the fish that of the Pandyas. It was not unnatural that the king who assumed the name 'Madurantaka' 'conqueror of the Pandyan capital Madura,' should adopt on his coins the Pandyan emblem of the fish in token of his sovereignty over the Pandyan country. The other coin of Uttama Chola has the Chera emblem, the bow, in addition to the fish and the tiger and has the legend in Devanagari characters and this coin has to be attributed to a later reign, that of Rajendra I, whose coins bearing the same emblems have the legend in Nagari, 'Sri Rajendrah.' There has always been a tendency in the Dravida country to pay increasing deference to the classical language, Sanskrit; and the period of the currency of the two coins above noticed could be determined by the change (from the Grandha to the Devanagari) in the characters used in inscribing the legend on the coins. One unique specimen has the legend in old Tamil 'Avanipa Sekaran Cholaha,' with two fishes on the obverse, but without any symbol to indicate that it had a Chola origin. In the Indian Antiquary for 1892, Dr. Hultzsch read the legend as 'Avanipa Sekaran Golaga,' and interpreted it to mean the round coin of 'Avanipa Sekaran,' but he was not quite certain of his reading. The absence of the dynastic emblem of the tiger is not peculiar to this coin alone, for, as will be presently pointed out, many of the coins of Raja Raja do not bear that emblem. It is not improbable that imitating the pronunciation of the Sanskrit 'Cholah' an attempt was made to transcribe the word in Tamil, in order that the legend might sound quite classical. It was unnecessary to show on the coin the Chola's dynastic emblem when the name of the king himself was given, while the two fishes on the obverse, indicated his supremacy in the Pandyan and Chola territories. On the other hand reading the legend as 'Golaga' and interpreting it as a 'round coin' would lead to the assumption that the perfectly superfluous information that the coin was round in shape, was conveyed by the legend, when the roundness of the coin was an obvious index of its shape. And the term 'gola' was itself one which could not have been paraded by a supreme sovereign having regard to its opprobrious significance in the Hindu Law. After Madurantaka alias Uttama Chola, came by far the greatest of the Chola kings, Raja Raja I, alias Raja Kesari Varma who ascended the throne in A.D. 985. He maintained a large standing army of well disciplined bodyguards, foot soldiers and archers, that was ever in readiness for active service, and with the aid of his valiant troops he quelled the rebellion of Kandalur Salai, subdued the Vengi and Ganga countries, defeated and humbled the Chalukyas, deprived the Pandyas of their splendour, took Ceylon and so distinguished himself. We read in one of his inscriptions, that he was worthy of worship everywhere. From 1001 A.D., he sheathed his sword and cultivated the arts of peace. When he ascended the throne, the Chola kingdom hardly comprised the districts of Trichinopoly and Tanjore and a portion of the district of Coimbatore. Before he died, he had destroyed the Chera fleet, his power extended over the whole of the modern Presidency of Madras, part of Mysore, the Island of Ceylon, the Laccadives and the Maldives. It was he who built the Brihatiswara Temple at Tanjore one of the grandest specimens of Dravidian architecture in Southern India. Though a great Saiva devotee he seems to have been tolerant of other sects and creeds. A set of twenty one copper plates, preserved now in the University Museum in Leyden in Holland, hence known as the Leyden Grant, records the interesting fact that he granted a village to a Buddhist Vihara at Negapatam, a monastery which was probably on the site of the present St. Joseph's buildings in that town. The regulations for the levy of taxes and the minuteness with which the land measurements were made indicate the great care bestowed by Raja Raja in the administration of the large empire which he had built up during his reign. From 1011 A.D. his son Rajendra ruled the country along with the father as heir apparent. The coins of Raja Raja also attest to the extent of his dominions and the length and prosperity of his rule, and throughout the Madras Presidency, we meet with his copper kasu in large numbers. Every itinerant pedlar who barters pepper, turmeric and spices for old copper is able to get together, after a week's labour, a large number of these specimens current more than nine hundred years ago. The commonest of these bear on their obverse a standing human figure clad in regal robes, and on the reverse the same figure seated, with the legend in Devanagari characters, 'Raja Raja' under the right arm. Coins with similar devices and legend occur also, but more rarely, in silver and gold. The Chola emblem, generally found on seals, is a seated tiger ; on the coins of the later Chola sovereigns, the figure of the seated tiger is found flanked by the fish, the Pandyan emblem and the bow, the Chera emblem. Yet this characteristic Chola device of the tiger is not generally to be found on the coins of Raja Raja. The only known instance in which the dynastic device is figured on his issues is a coin in impure silver, on the obverse of which is the typical squatting human figure above referred to with a seated tiger flanked by lamps and surmounted by a parasol, with on the reverse the seated tiger, the fish and the bow respectively, the Chola, Pandya and Chera emblems. On the other hand, the standing and seated human figures adverted to already are familiar symbols of the Sinhalese sovereigns of Ceylon, so much so that Raja Raja's coins are usually referred to as those of the Ceylon type. The adoption of this Ceylon type by Raja Raja, the greatest monarch of his age, must be of real significance. Might it not be that, to commemorate his victory over the king of Ceylon, and publish his supremacy in countries even beyond the seas, the device of the Sinhalese was adopted by their conqueror, the great Raja Raja Chola, just as the fish of the Pandya and the bow of the Chera were adopted to proclaim that he was a Mummudi Chola, or the Chola with the three crowns? Coins too are not uncommon on which the legend 'Raja Raja' appears along with the Pandyan emblem, the fish, and the Chalukyan emblem, the boar. The former coin has on the reverse also the legend 'Sekhara' written twice. The two gold pieces in plate VI, of distinctly Sinhalese type with the legends Lankêsvara and Raja Raja, were probably issued by this ambitious monarch in Ceylon after his conquest of the Island. At a later age Lankapura Dandanadha issued the Kahapanas of Ceylon after humbling the Pandyas, thus, history having its tale of reprisals and repetitions. Others there are attributable to this Chola king which bear distinctly Vaishnavite emblems such as the 'Vishnupāda', or feet of Vishnu, or the figure of Krishna as Muralidhara (the flute player,) familiar objects of worship among the Vaishnava sect. This fact is another instance of the king's religious toleration which made him endow a Buddhist monastery, and a Siva temple at about the same time. In still other specimens bearing the legend Raja Raja, there is on the obverse the representation of a gallopping horseman, but the significance of this symbol it is not yet possible to definitely determine. This diversity in the types of the coinage of Raja Raja tempts one to incline to the theory that the difference in type was the consequence of more than one prince of the same name having issued coins bearing the legend, Raja Raja. There was indeed more than one prince of the Chola kingdom bearing that name, but none so powerful or prosperous as the king who built the temple of Tanjore. It is therefore probable that the king when he conquered the Pandyas, ordered the fish emblems to be placed on the coins struck immediately after the victorious event, and a similar occasion might have prompted the adoption of the Chalukya and Simhalese devices, while the occurrence of Vaishnava and Saiva emblems alike on his issues serves to emphasize the extremely tolerant spirit that allowed of Vaishnava sculptures being wrought in the tower of the great Saiva Temple of Tanjore. Rajendra succeeded his father Raja Raja in 1011 A.D. and vanquishing the Ganga prince after a sanguinary war, assumed the surname of Gangai Konda Chola . Like his father, he was ceaseless in activity in humbling his rivals and annexing their dominions and making the Chola rule steadfast from Kalinga in the north to Kumari in the south. He it was who probably built the temple and settled in the place called after him, Gagaikonda Cholapuram, in the Wodaiyarpalayam Taluk of the Trichinopoly District. Like his father he took delight in parading in his inscriptions what was very likely a fact that he had humbled the Pandyas and Cheras. During his reign another intermarriage with the Chalukyas of Vengi served to further cement the relationship first brought about by the marriage of Raja Raja's daughter to a Chalukya prince. The coins of Gangai Konda Chola have the same devices both on the obverse and the reverse. 'In the centre is a seated tiger, the emblem of the Chola king, facing the right, with two fishes, the emblem of the Pandyan king in front, and a bow the emblem of the Chera king behind, the whole group flanked by two lamps and surmounted by a parasol and two chowries.' Underneath is the legend in Nagari 'Gangaikonda Chola' in two lines. The Collector of South Indian coins comes across now and then two other coins, one bearing the legend 'Sri Rajendra' and the other legend 'Uttama Chola' in Nagari characters both of the same type as the coins bearing the legend 'Gangaikonda Chola' already noticed. The first of these was evidently issued before the conquest of the Ganga country by Parakesari Varman, alias Rajendra Deva and the latter seems to have been issued when he assumed the surname Uttama Chola whenever that might have been. As already pointed out the title Uttama Chola was also assumed by Madurantaka, son of Gandaraditya, and the predecessor of Raja Raja. In the first half of the eleventh century five kings ruled between the time of Gangaikonda Chola and that of Kulôttunga Chola who ascended the throne in A.D. 1070. They all recount in their inscriptions in high sounding terms their warlike exploits and conquests over the neighbouring kingdoms. But there is a blank in the coinage of this period and no coins of these five sovereigns have hitherto beer discovered. In 1071 A.D. the daughter's son of Rajendra Chola, who was ruling from 1061 in Vengi or the Chalukya country usurped the Chola throne. He assumed the name, 'Kulôttunga Chola' and ruled over the southern country for nearly half a century. He had had been adopted by Rajendra alias Gangaikonda Chola as heir apparent to the throne, but only succeeded in obtaining the sovereignty by force in the year 1070 A.D., some nine years after he had become ruler of Vengi. The province of Vengi was thereafter entrusted by him to his uncle first, and then to his sons, one of whom Vira Chola assumed the office of Viceroy in 1078 A.D. Kulôttunga I conquered the Kerala, Pandya, and Kuntala countries and was anointed in the Chola kingdom as Kulôttunga Chola Deva. It is not possible without encroaching much on the reader's time, to recount the doings of Kulôttunga during a long reign. One remarkable title of his however cannot be omitted. He was quite as just as he was valiant and being struck with the oppressive character of the numerous tolls and taxes till then levied and under the weight which his people were groaning, he abolished the tolls altogether thus gaining the name of Sungam tavirta Kulôttunga Chola Deva—he who abolished the tolls. Kulôttunga resided both at Gangaikonda Cholapuram and Kanchipuram; the latter place which was only second in importance became a Chola city after the subversion of the Pallavas in the eighth century A.D. One would expect that such a long reign could be illustrated by a fairly large variety of coins but the results of numismatic research till now have been disappointing. Some years ago there was a find of sixteen gold coins in the Krishna District, which are now in the Government Central Museum at Madras. The Government Epigraphist, to whom they were sent, deciphered and published them in the Indian Antiquary. The coin is described as follows:—'Centre: A boar facing the proper left and surrounded by two lamps, an elephant goad, a parasol, and two indistinct emblems.' Margin, Sri Raja Raja Samwat-34. 'The coins bear the legend on the obverse, while the punchmarks show through on the plain reverse. The irregular concave shape of the obverse was evidently caused by the gradual bending of the coin during the application of six several punches to make the impressions on the coins.' In the same series have to be placed other coins which show on the obverse a boar and on the reverse the legend 'Chola Narayana.' The first of these is surmised by Dr. Hultsch to be that of Kulôttunga's father, the Eastern Chalukyan king, Raja Raja, who ruled between A.D. 1022-1063; while the latter is attributed to Kulôttunga himself from the fact that he had borne the surname, Rajanarayana. There are in my possession copper pieces which have on the obverse the standing figure, as in Raja Raja's coins, and on the reverse, a standing boar, with the Telugu or Canarese legend above, which may be read Cho and Nu . But unless better specimens are procured and further research throws more light on the coinage of this period, nothing definite can be stated about the reign in which the coin was issued. The Chola power after Kulôttunga I, began gradually to wane and the last king with any pretentions to power was Kulôttunga III, 1278, A.D. By the year 1234, A.D. we see a Hoysala king established in the Chola country with his capital at Kannanore near Samayapuram. We hear also that Raja Raja III was captured by a Perum Singa and had to be rescued by a Hoysala king who consequently prided himself by assuming the title of the ' Establisher of the Chola Kingdom.' At this time too, the Pandyan power which had so long been subject to the Cholas, received a fresh impetus under Mara Varman Sundara Pandya who boasts of having burnt Tanjore and Uraiyur, presented the Chola kingdom to a favourite, but when the Chola prostrated at his feet made a free gift of the kingdom to him. Thus we find in the end of the thirteenth century, the Cholas decline and fall, after having for nearly four centuries been the sole arbiters of the destinies of Dravida Desam. The coins belonging to this period of Chola sovereignty have not yet been found; but there are with me unassigned coins which possibly refer to the successors of Kulôttunga. On the obverse of all these is the standing Ceylon figure so often referred to above, while on the reverse is the figure of a standing bull, with the Nagari or Canarese syllable 'Vi' which may stand for 'Vikrama Chola', the immediate successor of Kulottunga alias Rajendra. It may not be improbable too that to the more than one Raja Raja that ruled after Kulôttunga we have to attribute the more modern looking of the copper issues bearing the legend Raja Raja. Some of the Pandyan coins of this period throw light on the low ebb to which the Chola power had been reduced by various causes. One coin bears the legend 'Kachi Vaḷangum Perumāl' which means that a Pandyan king after taking the Chola town Kanchipuram in battle, gave it back generously to the vanquished Chola prince. The other records that the Pandyan king conquered the Chola country, in the brief legend “Chōnāḍu Koṇdān.” Thus briefly is the story of the Chola coinage as far as it is known at present. By far the commonest of them are the copper cash of Rāja Rāja ; the gold and silver pieces are very difficult to obtain. The issues of a large number of the Chola sovereigns have yet to be discovered and deciphered. Vast quantities of these valuable store-houses of information are annually going ‘to the goldsmith’s crucible and the brazier’s melting pot’ and it is the duty of every earnest enquirer into the condition of Ancient India to rescue them from this cruel fate. title: The Origin of the Word Arya
author: V. J. Tamby Pillai
text: THE ORIGIN OF THE WORD 'ARYA' BY V. J. TAMBY PILLAI ESQ., M.R.A.S. ( Ceylon ) THE name 'Aryas' ( ) by which the Vedic race called itself in times of pre-historic antiquity seems to furnish a very important and interesting point of contact between that race and the primitive Dravidians. It is held to be a purely Sanscrit term derived from a primordial root akin to, or identical with, the Latin and Greek ar meaning 'to plough' and, hence, it has been inferred that, at first, it meant 'a cultivator', and then 'a lord' or 'a nobleman', which latter meaning it is said to retain till today. It may, however, be pointed out here that that eminent Sanscritist, the late Dr. K. M. Bannerjea of Calcutta, did not concur in the above explanation. He theorized that the word was originally of Semitic extraction but adopted into, and naturalized in, Sanscrit in later times. If the true history of the term and of its connexion with Sanscrit be that given by the learned Dr. Bannerjea, we need no further proof to show that the true 'Aryas' of antiquity were a race, not the same as that from which the primitive Sanscritians sprang. It is possibly a historical fact that the country beyond the Western frontier of the Punjab known as 'Ariana',* * Bochart proves that Media was called Ara or Aria from Hara, a place where the Assyrian kings Pul and Tiglathpilesar had vanquished the Reuvenites, the Gadites and the half tribe of Manasseh (vide I Chronicles. chap : 5, v. 26). The name Ariyan appears thus to be of Semitic origin, but adopted and naturalized in Sanscrit. 'A Turanian invasion of Media, as was suggested by Dr. Oppert, was probably the cause of the introduction of the name Media and the as Dr. Bannerjea says, for some centuries preceding the Christian era, was anciently inhabited by the forefathers of the later Sanscrit-speaking races of Hindustan. This forms, however, no irrefragable proof of any primordial connexion between the primitive Sanscritians and the name of 'Aryas' now applied to them. For, there is nothing to preclude the supposition that the country might have been so named on account of its having been the residence of a pre-Semitic or Turanian race long before it came into the possession of the ancestors of the Indic Sanscritians. Moreover, if the conclusion of many an antiquarian may be relied on that the ancient Semites were indebted to their neighbours for most of their culture and arts, we are not, then, wrong in carrying the pedigree of the art of husbandry further back to the times when the Bels of Chaldea ruled supreme in the regions of the Persian Gulf. Referring consequent expulsion of the Ariyans from their primitive home.' The Ariyan Witness by Rev. Dr. K. M. Bannerjea, pp. 83, 93 and 91.) If 'Hara', or 'Ara' was, in fact, the primitive yocable from which the word 'Arya' was in subsequent times evolved, the suggestion may not be out of place that the Tamils with whom the Brahminical races are admitted to have freely mixed were known also by a name significantly corresponding to 'Hara' or 'Ara'—I mean the name 'Arava' by which they are called even to-day by their neighbours. It is here necessary to refute the following dictum born of prejudice of the author of The Indian Empire , viz. 'many words have been borrowed (by the Indo-Aryan vernaculars) from Dravidian languages generally in a contemptuous sense. Thus the common word pilla , "cub," is really a Dravidian word meaning "son"." (vide p: 363). The above observation is obviously based on incorrect information. ' Pillai ' in Tamil means 'child' and not 'son' and is used to denote not only a human child but also the young of a parrot, a squirrel, a mungoose, a young cocoanut-palm a young areca-palm, &c., &c. There is no reason to doubt that 'pillai' was in ancient times used to signify not only a human child but also the young of all domesticated or pet animals of the Tamil people. To make the case stronger I would cite that of the word 'kulavi' (குலவி) which though now restricted in meaning to a human child was used also in ancient Tamil to connote the young of beasts. 'Kulavi' and 'pillai' are words meaning the same thing and their usages were most probably also similar. to the position of the pure Semites with regard to civilization, the great German savant, Dr. F. R. Grau of Konisburg says, 'If the idea of culture is understood in the sense in which the Hamites laid its foundations and the Indo-European erected thereon the magnificent structure of modern civilization, then the Semites as a whole must be excluded from the list of civilized nations. . . . For, while around them flourished various forms of Hamitic civilization, they were destitute of everything which could be compared with them; . . . (among them) no science, no art, was developed, no industry or even trade, sprang up.'* Is it probable, then, that the Aryans learnt the art of agriculture from the Semitic nomads? To quote Dr. Grau once more, 'Mankind owes to the Hamites the first great development of agriculture. It was not merely to the fertility of the low lands that their agricultural success was due, but rather to their rational system of management. An agricultural literature sprang up among the ancient Hamites, also at a very early period.'† The improbability, then, of a term meaning 'cultivator' first originating among a race of shepherds such as the Semites are known to have been, when they emerge in history, is a strong proof of its non-Semitic derivation. In so far as its relation to the dialect of the Vedic race is concerned, the following lines would seem to contain all that has hitherto been said about it by those who have believed in its Sanscritian origin, viz. the term 'Arya' in modern Sanscrit means 'noble,' or 'of good family', and it is probably connected with the root 'ar' which, in both Greek and Latin, means 'to plough' and which appears in English in the word 'ear-th' meaning literally 'what is ploughed' from an old English word 'to ear' meaning 'to plough'. The * The Goal of The Human Race , pp. 87-8. † The Goal of The Human Race , p. 6. Aryas. perhaps, it is further explained, used this word to distinguish themselves as an agricultural nation with a settled home from the wandering tribes of Tartars that surrounded them. It need hardly be pointed out that this theory is, at best, a mere conjecture as no satisfactory proof has yet been added to show that 'Arya' ever meant, in primitive Sanscrit, 'a husbandman', or that agriculture was, at any time, regarded by the primitive Sanscritians as a noble occupation. For while 'the Hamites settled in fruitful and alluvial plains' well-suited for agriculture, 'the Indo-Europeans preferred mountains and heights unfavourable for developing the first germs of civilization.' 'The primitive Indo-European nation was, probably, still in that peculiar state of transition in which agriculture is only temporarily carried on and is subordinated to cattle breeding as it is now the case among many Arab tribes.'* It will thus be seen that the great agricultural races of the ancient world were necessarily of the Hamitic or Cushite stock, and that, if the primitive Sanscritians were ever indebted to any race for their knowledge of systematic husbandry, these must have been a Cushite people and not Semites. Further, no trace of the supposed pre-eminence of the agricultural class amongst the primitive Sanscrit-speaking tribes can be shown to exist in their language or writings, and this fact, considering the great amount of old literature in Sanscrit that has come down to our day, seems fatal to any supposition or inference that the term 'Arya' was primarily the tribal name of the agricultural fore-fathers of the Sanscritic Indians. Are we able to glean any evidence from Sanscrit literature that the cultivating classes at any time held the highest rank in the social arrangements of the ancient Sanscritians? The answer to this question is neither * The Goal of The Human Race , pp. 6, 57-8. difficult nor far to seek. In their social and political organization, it was the priest who, it is commonly believed, held the foremost place, while, the cultivator was, in point of rank or precedence, considered lower than even the rude swordsman who often led the life of a free-booter or marauder.* The impossibility of deriving an honoured name from that of a despised class is too evident to be mistaken and unless it can be proved that the mass of literature in Sanscrit presents things in a way quite the reverse of what they actually were in times of old, the suggestion that the 'Aryas' were, at first, a race of farmers must be abandoned as utterly groundless. Sir M. M. William, in his Indian Wisdom , says, 'the very name Arya is, as every one now knows, connected with the root ri=ar , whence aratrum , 'a plough,' (e.g. Sanscrit aritra ). It is curious to note how the Brahmans, after their segregation as the dominant class, sought to deprecate agriculture. Manu (X. 84) says: 'Some think that agriculture ( krishi ) is an excellent thing, but it is a mode of existence blamed by the good, because the iron-mouthed plough-share wounds the earth and the creatures living in it.' To this, the author of The Vedic India , which may be said to be a summary, in many important respects, of the conclusions and inferences arrived at by a large number of Indo-logists of European reputation, replies as follows, viz: 'it has been suggested — but the attractive suggestion has unfortunately not proved capable of sufficient scientific proof — that the name " Arya " itself is connected with this root (e.g. ar= to plough,) and the people who took it for their own originally meant to call themselves "the people who plough" in proud distinction from their sheep-raising, steppe-roaming, the * In Bengal where Brahminical influences have been strong for some centuries past, the cultivating classes, the Mahisyas, held a lower place than the Banias, the traders, till the times of (Ballal Sen Ballala-Sena), a king of the last dynasty of Bengal who were Vellala princes of Southern India. This king raised the Mahisyas, it is said, over the Banias thus changing the social usages of old Bengal in conformity with the practices of the Tamils. robber neighbours, the Turanians. But, at the time at which we begin to know them Arya meant noble, exalted, venerable.* It is well known to students of history that 'upon the fall of Carthage, the Romans handed over to their African allies the libraries of their fallen foes, retaining, however, the great work of Mago, a contemporary of Cyrus, on agriculture which consisted of twenty-eight volumes, and dealt with all branches of the art. It was, subsequently, at the request of the Senate, translated into Latin. But, Carthage, in this as in other branches of culture, was merely the missionary and intermediary of the Babylonians and the Egyptians. The existence of the book of Nabathaean agriculture proves beyond doubt that the art of husbandry was highly developed in ancient Chaldea while there exists positive monumental evidence of the times of "The Ancient Empire" of Egypt that it was then in a state of high development in that country.'† In the opinion of the famous Liebig, modern people can rival the Mongolian Chinese in their rational method of agriculture, while Sir John Hewett, in his treatise on The Pre-historic Ruling Races says that the Dravidians were, of all the great races of antiquity, the first to systematize agriculture. The Rig-Veda is supposed to be a very ancient book. Some scholars have even ascribed to certain hymns of its earlier chapters an antiquity far higher than the time of the entrance of the ancestors of the Sanscritic Indians into the land of the Five Rivers—an antiquity co-eval with the times when the remote ancestors of the Vedic Rishis lived in peace and comfort in their primordial habit at near the North Pole offering sacrifices and singing hymns to their god or gods or powers of nature.‡ Now, the word 'Arya' * Vedic India , by Z. A. Ragozin, pp. 6-12. † The Goal of The Human Race , pp. 6. 7. ‡ In the Rig Veda the race which called itself Aryas is referred to as 'the descendants of Manu', 'the tribes of Nahush', 'the five tribes of Nahush' frequently occurs in the hymns of the Rig , and if its composition really dates in that far-off age of the past when the common progenitors of the Sanscritic Indians, the Greeks, the Latins, the Schlaves, the Kelts, and the Teutons yet lived together in regions outside the boundaries of India, it follows that the use of the appellation 'Arya' must have been equally current among the early European races belonging to these nationalities as among those whose descendants called themselves by that name on the plains of Hindustan. But, strangely enough, not one of these European races who, by the affiliation of language, have been proved to belong to the same ethnological stock with the Sanscritic Indians now remembers, or have preserved even, the slightest trace of the fact of their being once known by the name of 'Aryas'; and this is even still more strange and inexplicable in the case of the Hellenistic and the Latin races, as it seems most probable that if the term did actually exist in the old common mother tongue of the Indo-Aryan group of races, it would have found a place in the rich vocabulary of ancient Greece which possessed a literature reaching far back, it is said, into 'the five tribes—Yadus, Duruvasus, Duruhyus, Anus and Purus', 'the worshippers of Indra' &c., &c., &c. Besides 'Yadus and Duruvasus', says Mr. Lewis Rice, 'Yayati had three sons, Drahyu, Anu and Puru and the collective people of the five races who claimed to be descended from these were the Dravidian Bharatas under Visvamitra who resisted the Aryan advance under Vashishta.' (Vide The Gazetter of Mysore by Lewis Rice M.A., Chap: on Ethnology.') The author of the Vedic India writing almost in the same strain says that the Baharatas and the Purus were originally Dravidians. ( Vedic India , pp. 328, 319, 324). Add to the above the tradition that the progenitor Manu who with seven others survived the deluge was, according to the Puranas in which are preserved undoubtedly the traditions and myths of pre-historic Bharathavarsha, a king of the Dravida country of the race of the Pandyas. It may be noted also that Yadu and Duruvasu, whom the Puranas, the Tamil liturature and South Indian inscriptions connect with the Dravidians, are always mentioned together in the Rig Veda and lived in the regions of the Yamuna on the banks of which the ancient Madura is said to have been rounded by the ancestors of the Pandyas. antiquity. This applies as well to the Latin language which is equally guiltless of possessing any evidence that the term 'Arya' was a household name of the primitive Romans. Some have ventured by artificial and fanciful derivations and explanations to connect terms which, in form, are utterly unlike one other. As an instance of these feats of philology, I would just repeat* what Mr. Kunte, who was a staunch believer in the common origin of the Sanscritic Hindus, and the old Greeks and the Teutons of Europe, has stated on this point. He says 'Arya', when it is pronounced, as a Londoner pronounces 'arm' into 'harm', becomes 'harya', and being slightly modified, it passed into 'Hellas' the name of the Hellas. 'Hellaspont' i.e. Ariapatha was so named on account of its being the highway of the 'Aryas'. The Germans converted the 'Harya' into 'Herr' which has passed into 'Sir' of the English language. Some insignificant tribes pressed from behind by stronger Aryas, penetrated into Italy, and settled in its different parts husbanding their energy, but occupying the fertile portions of the peninsula under different names. Hence, there is no name in Latin that exactly corresponds to 'Arya' in sound, or sense.† And likewise, the ancient Schalves also had no remembrance of their * The Vicissitudes of Aryan Civilization of India , by M. M. Kunte, B.A., pp. 66-7. † A close parallel to the absence of the term 'Arya' in the Teutonic Latin and Schlavonic tongues of Europe is furnished by the Sanscrit word 'Sahasra' meaning 'thousand'. 'There is no common word says' Z. At Rogozin 'for thousand in our languages or more correctly in the parent languages of ours—Sanscrit, Greek, Latin', Old Teutonic having each fabricated a word of its own . . . as to our Aryan forefather, we cannot escape the inference from this fact that they could count only up to a hundred-the numerals so far coinciding in all Aryan languages with almost comical regularity; . . . they may have known of thousands as so many 'tens of hundreds,' and counted . . . twelve hundred, eighteen hundred and so on.' The Vedic India p. 73. The above seems to be a conclusive proof of the Sanscrit 'Sahasra' being a modified form of the Tamil 'Aiyiram' 'thousand' the intermediate steps being 'Sayiram, Sasiram, and Sahasiram. once being 'Aryas.' These are opinions, which, in view of the great names that support them, cannot, I admit, be despised. It may, however, be observed that if the evolution of the 'Aryapatha' of the Brahmans into the 'Hellespont' of the Greeks be a fact, the day cannot be far distant when we shall be told to believe that the 'Ravaneswara' of the South Indian Kurumbas is only an evolved form of the 'Unkulun-Kulu' of the South African Zulus. Having been so far concerned with the term 'Arya' in its Sanscritic relations , we shall now proceed to enquire if it is possible to connect it with any Dravidian source. It is now generally admitted that the Vedic Sanscritians were not at all a pure race, their ancestors having freely intermarried with the pre-Aryan tribes who opposed their advance into the plains of the Ganges. It was pointed out years ago by Dr. Taylor that a Tamiloid language, now represented by its most cultivated branch in the South, constituted the original staple of all the languages of India. The existence of a Tamilian substratum in all the modern dialects of India and of the profound influence which the classical Tamil has exercised on the formation and development of both the Vedic and the classical Sanscrit, is gradually coming to be recognized by students of Indian philology. Further, modern investigations have shown that the bulk of the population of Northern India, so far as their racial affinities are concerned, contain a common factor essentially Dravidian in blood. Says an eminent authority: 'From an ethnological point of view, the Aryans of India are not a pure race as they appear to have been when they dwelt in the valley of the Indus; for, in the Veda , a contrast is often drawn between a clear complexion and the dark skin of the indigenous people. They must, on the contrary, have mixed with the natives at some period when a peculiar civilization was in development, and not only has the physical type greatly altered its original Indo-European character, but the whole civilization of the Indians has received the stamp of Southern and Eastern Asia which makes them appear to us even stranger than the Asiatic Semites or the Egyptians. This fact is often overlooked, because the use of the Aryan speech continually reminds us of the close relationship between the Indian Aryans and the Persians and Europeans; and it is not merely that the Aryans have assumed the racial marks of the Dravidians, but, on the other hand, the pure type of the indigenous population has only been preserved in the uncivilized mountain peoples.* If in this mixture of the races and the languages of ancient India, we see the origin of a Sanscritic Dravidian race in the north of India, many centuries anterior to our era, it becomes easy to explain how the Tamil term 'Aryan' came to be adopted into the primitive Sanscrit. It is also by no means improbable that the primitive abodes of the two races were in contiguous regions, and that the process of miscegenation had already been in progress when they started on their journey towards the frontiers of the Punjab. Again, the literature, traditions and the customs of the Tamilians support the pre-eminent respectability of the calling of husbandry and hence it is that the social distinctions observed among them have been essentially different from those prevailing among the races of Northern India. To the Dravidian, there was, indeed, nothing nobler than the yoke and the plough which were to him the very emblems of freedom, honour and virtue. In his estimation, he only was a real freeman to whom the plough was the sole means of livelihood, while all others were, in fact, only servants. That a word once meaning 'a farmer' among such people should have, in the course of time, come to signify 'a noble person' would, therefore, seem to be nothing difficult to * The Historians' History of the World —'Indian History in Outline' Chapter I, 'Land and People', p. 489. appreciate.* It is remarkable that the Tamil êt ( çî ) assumes the form âr ( çî ) in Kanarese from which ûriyar ( çflwî ) in the sense of 'cultivators' is easily derived. The Hala (Old) Kannada in which the older literature of the Kornatas is written preserves, undoubtedly, many primitive forms and expressions of the parent-tongue of the Tamilians, and the Kanarese âr ( çî ) represents, possibly, the more ancient form of the word. If it be contended, however, that 'Arya' really meant in Sanscrit not 'husbandman' but 'a noble person,' it is hardly more necessary than to invite attention to the detailed discussion of this point in an earlier issue of this journal† in which an endeavour was made to prove that 'Aryan' ( çflwç ) meaning 'a great or exalted person' is Tamil in origin. If one only keeps in view the fact that Tamil is by far older‡ than Sanscrit, and that the latter even in its earlier * 'Amongst the pure Tamils the class most honoured was that of the Arivar or 'sages.' Arivar were ascetics: but of the men living in society the farmers occupy the highest position. They formed the nobility or the landed aristocracy of the country. They are now known as Mudalis or 'the first caste.', ( The Tamils Eighteen Hundred Years Ago , pp. 113-4.) 'Their (the Tamils') civilization was certainly older than that of the Aryas, for amongst the latter the fighting men were next in rank to the priests, whereas among the Tamils the farmers were next to the religious men, the military class was below even that of the herdsmen and artisans. . . To this day the Vellala does not take meals or drink water at the house of a Padaiyatchi, who calls himself a Kshatriya or a merchant who passes for a Vaisya' (Vide ibidem , p. 116.) † The Tamilian Antiquary No. I, pp. 45-9. (2nd Edition, pp. 42-3.) ‡ It (Tamil) stands alone without any immediate predecessor. In origin it must be long anterior to the Sanscrit. Professor Rhys Davids, in his Buddhistic India , commenting on the evolution of the Aryan languages of India, maintains that the Vedic Sanscrit is largely mixed up with the primitive Dravidian. There is little doubt that the Dravidian languages are incomparably older in point of time than Sanscrit. It is not an unreasonable supposition that they once occupied the whole of Hindustan and have been driven to stages of growth contained a large admixture of the primitive Dravidian, the strangeness of the phenomenon of the Aryo-Dravidian* or Vedic race of old calling itself by a name indigenous to India must, in a large measure, disappear. their present position to the South and along the coast by the encroachment of other languages coming from the north-west. (Vide, The Manual of the Administration of the Madras Presidency , by Dr. Maclean, pp. 42, 112-3). * 'We may assume for our present purpose that the ancestors of the Indo-Aryans came into India from the north-west and that at the time of their arrival the Peninsula, as far as the valley of the Ganges and the Jumna, was in the possession of the Dravidians. . . For the origin of the Aryo-Dravidian type we need not travel beyond the ingenious hypothesis put forward by Dr. Hoernle twenty years ago and confirmed by the recent researches of Dr. Grierson's Linguistic Survey. This theory supposes that after the first swarm of Indo-Aryans had occupied the Punjab, a second wave of Aryan-speaking people, the remote ancestors of the Aryo-Dravidians of to-day, . . made their way into India through Gilget and Chitral and established themselves in the plains of the Ganges and Jumna the sacred middle-land (Madhyadesa) of post-Vedic tradition. Here they came in contact with the Dravidians; . . here the Vedas were composed and the whole fantastic structure of orthodox ritual and usage was built up. The linguistic evidence in favour of this view is summarized in Dr. Grierson's chapter on Language in the Report on the Census of India, 1901. For the present purpose it is sufficient to note that the record of physical characters bears out the conclusions suggested by philology. The type of the people now dwelling in the middle-land is precisely what might have been expected to result from the incursion of a fair, long-headed race travelling by a route which prevented women from accompanying them, into a land inhabited by dark-skinned Dravidians. The men of the stronger race took to themselves the women of the weaker, and from these unions was evolved the mixed type which we find in Hindustan and Bihar. 'It (this theory) explains how it is that the Vedic Hymns contain no reference to the route by which the Aryans entered India or to their earlier settlement on the Indus; and it accounts for the antagonism between the eastern and the western sections and for the fact that the latter were regarded as comparative barbarians by the more cultured inhabitants of the middle-land.' (Vide Imperial Gazetteer of India . The Indian Empire, Vol. I, New Edition, pp. 300, 303-4.)

title: The Canarese War
author: T. Ponnambalam Pillai
text: THE CANARESE WAR* BY T. PONNAMBALAM PILLAI ESQ., M.R.A.S. I N spite of the fact that the Dravidians were the possessors of a civilization even more ancient than that of the Aryans, the history of that part of India occupied by them is still enshrouded in mystery. It is to be regretted that even the times within the memory of man are in that cimmerian darkness. Any attempt to remove this veil should be welcome. While I had been making researches in the history of this ancient land, I came across a cultured young gentleman—a scion of an ancient family in South Travancore which gave a Prime Minister to that estate—who had been silently working towards the same end. He placed at my disposal a few manuscripts of popular songs, which certain classes of people in that part of the country sing in the months of November and December, to the accompaniment of a lyre in the form of a bow, which has consequently given the poems the name of Vil Adichan Pattu meaning songs of the beater of bow, and requested me to make out what I could with the aid of the scanty knowledge of Tamil I possessed. The heading of the most important of the manuscripts is ' Cannadian Pêr ' (കണ്ഠമുധന്ത പോറി) which means the War of the Canarese. The verses are evidently in heroic metre and I do not think they are to be found committed to writing. The copies before me were taken down as they were recited. * With kind permission reprinted from the Wednesday Review .—Ed. — through the efforts of my young friend, in the form they were handed down from mouth to mouth by the unlettered. They, therefore, defy all rules of grammar and prosody, though there are sure signs of their having conformed to them once. The poem gives an account of an unreturned royal love, and the consequent invasion of the dominions of the offending monarch. The actual scene of operations was between South Travancore, and a line drawn in the Tinnevelly District from Tuticorin to Shermadevi, and from there to the hills which form part of the Western Ghauts. The difficulty that would confront one in a matter like this is the assigning of dates to the events narrated in the folk songs. From the fact that the expedition was despatched by the Canarese king of Mysore, it is but natural to conclude that he must have belonged to the Nava-Bellala dynasty which became extinct towards the close of the fourteenth century of the Christian era. Again from the fact that an embassy was despatched to the Chera king at Tiruvanjikalam, one may be tempted to carry the events to a time before the tenth century. But as the Vijayanagar kings were of Vaduga and Cannada descent, it is likely that the king referred to was of that line, and the generals referred to were some of his own or of the Naick Viceroys of Madura. I believe, the latter is the view of Professor Rengaswamy Iyengar of the Maharajah's College, Trivandram, and it is what I infer from an article of Mr. V. Rangachariar that appeared in the Wednesday Review of the 2nd February, 1910. In case the events are assigned to the Naick period, they must have transpired during the time of Viswanath Naick, the founder of the dynasty. For, it was he that fought with the last of the Pandyas; the chief participators in the military operations as recorded in the manuscripts were the Canarese Generals, on one side, and the members of the Pandyan family stationed at Va||iyūr, in the Nanguneri Taluq of the Tinnevelly District and eleven miles from the borders of Travancore, on the other. I shall not say further on the subject and leave it to others more competent. Now to the story as given in the manuscripts. The ministers of Kulasêkhara Pândyan, fearing an attack from the Canarese Generals, advised their king to retire to his southern capital Va||iyûr, and so he did. About this time some minstrels going about from house to house to earn their livelihood by singing popular songs and exhibiting representations of men and places, one day obtained admittance into the Canarese court, and depicted in high-flown metres the personal accomplishments of the Pandyan, and made an effective scenic representation of his likeness before the maiden daughter of the king. She at once became infatuated with love, repaired to the august presence of her father, and spoke in unequivocal terms that either she should make the young Kulasêkhara as her wedded lord or become herself a prey to fire. The king was alarmed at the attitude of his daughter; and without losing time, he despatched an envoy offering Kulasêkhara her hand along with the kingdom that extended from 'Benares to Cape Comorin' and 'all the paraphernalia belonging to that exalted position'. The envoy started at once on his eventful mission and, after traversing various parts of the ancient Chola and Pandyan kingdoms, reached Valliyur where he was ushered into the royal presence at the appointed time, and in due form. When he was interrogated as to the object of his mission, he stated it. The Pandyan scoffed at the idea of making an alliance with a family that was of plebian origin, and with which his ancestors had not formed any connection. The envoy pressed the request of his employer; but the prince was inexorable, and told him to go about his business. He, however, took care to observe the etiquette of his court and to command his ministers to make him the usual presents before dismissing him. Disappointed and crest-fallen as he was, the Canarese envoy left the Pandyan court and reached Dwarasamudram in eighteen days and related all that had taken place. While doing so, he gave a graphic account of the Pandyan country, his great cities including his capital, his fort, his court and his personal accomplishments. The daughter of the king as she listend to it with wrapt attention, became still more infatuated, and pined away so as to lose her health. Intimation was given to her father as to the state of her health. He sent for his daughter and, assuring her that he would endeavour to secure Kulasekhara for her husband, despatched the same envoy on a second mission to secure the object in view. Kulasekhara reaffirmed his previous reply, and peremptorily ordered the royal messenger to clear out of his presence. On this the Pandyan Prime Minister proposed to put him to disgrace, but the prince declined to be a party to such an unkindly act. The Minister, however, took occasion to read a sermon to the envoy to impress upon him the antiquity of the royal line unlike that of his employer and the great prowess of the Pandyan dynasty in the art of war, not to say of its skill in the arts of peace. The ambassador again returned to Mysore disappointed, and related to his king all that had taken place. The result was a declaration of war. The King collected a large army composed of different nationalities from all parts of the empire from 'Benares to Cape Comorin' and set out with it on an auspicious day, after propitiating the deities for the success of his arms. His daughter was an important factor in the camp and she was there ready to wed the accomplished Kulasekhara, as soon as he fell into the trap laid by her father. The results of the war were not attained in a day, for it was a protracted struggle. It may be divided into three compaigns:— First: Up to the fall of Vailliyür Fort. Second: The rule of Othachy ( Othachy ), brother of the Canarese king as Viceroy, over Valliyür and the desultory warfare that took place for a long period. It closed with his death, and the retaking of the fort of Vaĥliyūr by the Pandyan armies. Third: The defeat of the last of the Pandyans and extermination of that dynasty. I shall deal with each campaign one by one. The first was not of short duration. It extended for about a year. The march of the Mysore army through the Chōla dominions was smooth-sailing as there were no opposing forces. In the Pandyan kingdom too, some semblance of authority was maintained only towards the extreme south. Till the army reached Poĥtaputhūr (which in reality is Vaĥtaputhūr w̄d̄d̄p̄l̄ḡāi ) there were no encounters. The Pandyan army was concentrated in that place, and the various divisions of it were placed under the command of four brothers and a nephew of Kulasēkhara. In the battle that ensued, the Canarese force was defeated, and it took refuge at Vaĥukachymalai ( w̄d̄s̄k̄s̄m̄w̄ ). As it was nearer to Vaĥliyūr the Pandyan army marched on to that place, to concentrate all its strength, and make a determined stand. Operations were commenced early on the following morning, and the respective forces were led by the nephews of the two kings. After a well-contested battle in which a large number of Mysoreans were left dead on the field, the Canarese were completely routed, and they again took refuge at Vaĥukachymalai. Finding the disconcerted state in which his daughter was, the Canarese king assured her that he would leave no stone unturned to compass her object. The next thing he did was to propitiate the evil spirits. While he was engaged in that pursuit with his immense force, spies informed Kulasēkhara that the attention of his enemy was diverted. He ordered his generals to attack him and they accordingly did so. The battle was again hotly contested. When arrays of Canarese men were discomfited, they were readily and persistently replaced by others. The victory was however with the Pandyan army. There was a pause. The Canarese generals were refitting their army by collecting all the stragglers and deserters together, and by replacing those slaughtered in the field, by means of levies from Mysore. But their king was again engaged in propitiating the evil spirits, and using the 'black art' to secure victory. On consulting a traitorous astrologer who seceded from the Pandyan camp, he declared in favour of the Mysoreans. While these events were transpiring in the camp of the Canarese king, the Pandyan was seeking a place of refuge in case of reverse. The chief minister Kālingavillan advocated the occupation of the fort at Chorimuttan-pārai (சேரிலுத்தன்பான்ற) in the possession of Chêra. It is one that was once built by the Pandyân, and had a zig-zig approach in which lay its safety. It appears to have gone into the hands of Chêra, as a result of conquest. His sanction was therefore necessary to occupy it. Though the Pandyan hesitated to go into the fort at the Chorimuttan-pārai, he did send his women and treasure. This place is in the Zemindary of Chingampatty, not far away from the sacred falls of Banathirtham . The manuscripts referred to communications with Neḍumangād, which is twelve miles from Trevandrum on one side and the Malayankulam (மழையான்குளம்) plains on the other. In Travancore, Neḍumangād is the nearest inhabited point that can be reached from Chorimuttan-pārai, through the Ponmudi Hills and Kallar . Malayankulam is about seven miles from Ambasamudram at the foot of the ghauts on the eastern side and it came into possession of the Travancore sovereigns probably as the successors of the last of the Pandyans. Till 1831 it was with that kingdom, but was ceded about that time to the British Government. All that is now left of the sovereignty of it are two ruined temples, the presiding dieties of which are receiving starvation allowance. Kulasêkhara was now free to fight, having got rid of all encumbrances. The Mysoreans were also ready after a lapse of six months to resume hostilities. Early on a morning the Canarese force laid siege to the fort of Vaḷḷiyūr. The Pandyan army defended it with all the might in its power. The brothers of the king and his nephew with the leading generals were posted at each of the fort gates. The battle raged fiercely. The armies were composed of infantry, cavalry, and elephant trains. The weapons that were used were bows and arrows, swords and lances. At the heat of the battle, the Pandyan thought that it was not fair to have the fort gates closed, and he accordingly caused them to be opened. The Canarese entered the fort. When the two opposing forces closed together there was hand to hand fight. In the hotly contested combat, the nephew (sister's son) of the Pandyan was slain. Though this event paralysed the action for a time, it emboldened him to try further conclusions. He therefore took the command himself, and led 40,000 horses, into the heart of the opposing army which spread itself between Vaḷḷiyūr and Vaḍukachymalai. This was one of the most sanguinary engagements, as it was one of vengeance. Kulasēkhara himself slew a large number of his enemies—men and horses, and the son of the Canarese king himself fell a victim to his sword. And the Cararese army was panic-stricken and fled, leaving the killed and wounded there. It seems that the soldiers of the defeated army were driven out as far as Veeravanallūr and the king and his staff encamped themselves with the remnant of his men on the plains of Callūr. It must be noted here that throughout the struggle, though the Pandyan army was victorious, the false steps taken by the king and his ministers had all the effects of a defeat. Even after this battle Kulasēkhara was advised to quit Vaḷḷiyūr and seek the stronghold where he had sent his women and treasure. He was personally averse to taking such a step, but the force of circumstances compelled him to accept the proferred advice. The Canarese army followed on his heels and a battle ensued in which the Pandyan king lost another great general in the person of his brother—Tikkelām Pugalum Perumāl (திக்கேலாம் பக்கும் பெருமான்). There was a lull. The Canarese army was encamped on the plains of Malayankulam and the Pandyan continued to remain in his aery at Chorimuttan-pārai. Both were unwilling to attack each other. The Canarese king tried to inveigle the Pandyan to descend to the plains from his fastness, and give one more battle, but his attempt was doomed to failure. After remaining inactive at the place for months he made up his mind to repair to Valīyiūr, and set his brother on the throne of Kulasēkhara. Accordingly he went to the place, put his brother in charge of Valīyiūr and returned to Mysore. Second Campaign :—Kulasēkhara Pandyan spent some years at Chorimuttan-pārai, and afterwards established himself at Thōvālai, in South Travancore, constructing a fort there, and extended his rule as far as Kōttār. Thus some years passed. The Canarese Viceroy at Valliyūr, Othachy, had not forgotten the aim of his brother, whose daughter yet remained a virgin, expecting to obtain the hand of Kulasēkhara. Information reached him of the movement of Kulasēkhara. He collected a large army and encamped at Muppandal close to the present frontiers of Travancore. On hearing this, the Pandyan prepared himself to meet him, and at the same time detatched a force to Kōttār that it may not be taken by a coup de main . The Mysoreans gradually approached the fort of Thōvālai and besieged it. A cannonade was opened and at last a breach was made in the wall. The Canarese men entered the fort and a fierce encounter took place. The Pandyan men wavered. While the zeal was flagging, timely assistance was afforded by the archers of Quilon and the lancers composed of the Ambalapulai Panikers. The situation was changed. The Mysoreans now faltered. They were routed and driven as far as Ilanguḷam (இளக்குளம்) and their leader was left dead in the field. After this victory Kulasēkhara re-entered the fort of Valīyiūr and took charge of his lost kingdom. Third Campaign: —Due intimation was conveyed to the Canarese king at Mysore of what had transpired. It was too much for him to bear. He at once started with a large army vowing vengeance, traversed the Chola and Pandyan countries as fast as he could, reached Mankaikād (மந்பைக்கொடு), united his forces with those of his late brother and engaged the Pandyan army on the plains of Mānāmguḷam (மாலுத்குளம்) and fought valiantly. Kulasēkhara and his brother knew that they were fighting for their life, and they behaved therefore in the battlefield with admirable courage. The carnage was terrible. Pachai-Perumal and Peria-Odayar, two of the brothers of Kulasēkhara, sacrificed their lives heroically. This proved an incentive to the Pandyan and his surviving brothers to fight more valiantly. They went on hacking to pieces the enemy's men. The bloodshed was terrible. But the opposing forces were overwhelming. The Pandyan applied to Chèra for assistance, but for some unaccountable reason it was not granted. At last he was compelled to retreat to Vaḷliyūr towards evening. Very early on the following morning he left it for his fastness with his immediate followers, and his valuables, leaving his remaining brothers and generals to continue the fight; at dawn on the following day hostilities were resumed, and they were carried on with the same vigour as on the previous day. The brothers and the leading generals except Kālingavillan (காவித்கவில்லன்) fell fighting desperately. On receiving intimation of the long expected catastrophe, Kulasēkhara thought that it was but right that he should proceed to the battlefield and take up the command of the army; but he felt that he was not destined to return. He therefore summoned all his seven wives to the side of the tank where he used to perform his ablutions, mentioned to them the errand on which he was going and requested them to remain in the fort with peace of mind till his return. But they knew what was to happen to their lord and king, and told him that they would rather lay their hand on their own lives, than be in a state of suspense. The king then assured them of meeting them in a week's time in a different sphere, and assented to the course proposed to be adopted by them. At this, the ladies entered the tank and drowned themselves. When the king was sure that life was extinct he caused the bodies to be placed on funeral pyres. After they were reduced to ashes, and performing the necessary rites, he found that he greatly relieved in mind and proceeded to the battle-field. There he found his faithful minister and commander-in-chief, Kälingavillan, awaiting his arrival. He requested the Pandyan for permission to take the command and it was granted. He fought most bravely for hours and brought down with his hand many heroes, and he himself succumbed at last. It was then the turn of Kulasêkhara, and he performed his duty with alacrity, and fought with the courage characteristic of his race. The Canarese king knew what the Pandyan was about, and warned his men against doing any harm in any way to his person. To enable them to approach him and sieze him without harming him, and themselves, he enjoined them to wearmail-coats. After a sanguinary encounter they surrounded him, made a captive of him put him in a palanquin, closed it carefully and took the valuable prize to their-master. In the flush of success it did not occur to the Canarese warriors, to disarm their prisoner. For he had a pocket knife, and with it he cut his throat on the way, and put an end to his life. As soon as the Pandyan was made a prisoner, that news was conveyed to the camp of the Canarese king, where he and his daughter were rejoicing over the event and loaded with presents those who took the glad tidings. The precious treasure in the palanquin was being momentarily expected, and when it reached the royal presence what was found was only the mortal remains of the last of the Pandyans. The princess viewed it with composure and realized that the account given to her by the ministrels of the personal accomplishments of Kulasêkhara was in no way exaggerated. She reconciled herself to her fate, and requested her father to cremate the body and allow her to ascend the funeral pyre, as if she were the wedded wife of the Pandyan. It was granted and another tragedy was brought to a close. The account which has just been concluded is no fable. Though the manuscripts are full of exaggerations and supernaturalisms, I have sifted what I considered to be historical facts. The three South Indian dynasties were connected with one another from time immemorial by marriage, and about the eleventh century A. D. the Chola and the Pandyan became merged into one another. At the present moment no traces of them are to be found anywhere, for both the races have become extinct. Owing to conquest and other causes the original stock was corrupted and the hybrids of the main lines ceased to exist early, while the collaterals lingered here and there with a show of some vitality. These also collapsed as in the case of the Pandyan family at Vaĥliyūr.

title: Tamil Proverbs
author: J. Lazarus
text: TAMIL PROVERBS* BY THE REV. DR. J. LAZARUS The Tamil language abounds in proverbs. The people take special delight in quoting them. The fact that about 10,000 old sayings and similes that were published in my work, under the title of Dictionary of Tamil Proverbs proves the richness of Tamil proverbial literature. No one can speak to a Tamilian without coming across a proverb or two. This is especially the case with Tamil women. Whether for purposes of approval or rebuk, satire or appeal, figure or illustration, truth or precept, or even mere negation or assertion, a proverb is ever at their command. Old women are so very familiar with them that they often argue by means of proverbs. Even 'yes' and 'no' are expressed in similes. This desire on the part of the people for the constant use of proverbs in ordinary talk, on the one hand, and the wealth of their poetic as well as proverbial literature, on the other, indicate the great antiquity and poetic nature of the Tamil people. It is said that the members of the Madura College used to ask and answer questions in perfect verse. A proverb has been defined as the 'wisdom of many and the wit of one.' Ray, who was the first to publish a complete list of English proverbs, defines a proverb as 'a short sentence or phrase in common use, containing some trope, figure, homonym, rhyme or other novelty of expression.' The Tamil word for proverb means simply 'an old saying'; which is in itself an excellent definition. * Reprinted from Rev. Dr. J. Lazarus' "From an Indian Garden" with kind permission. The most usual, and, in my opinion, the best form of a Tamil proverb is an iambic tetrameter, with a rhyme in the first and third feet. Thus, agattil alagu mugattil teriyum , 'the beauty of the mind is seen in the face.' Sometimes alliteration takes the place of the rhyme as in the following: káytta maram kalladi padum , 'it is the tree laden with fruit that is pelted with stones.' The saying may be destitute of both these ornaments, as in, âru kadantâl nîyár nánár? 'after the river is crossed, who are you and who am I?' Still there is a rhythm which gives it grace and smoothness. Some proverbs are also double tetrameters, while others again are simple diameters. But whatever form a proverb may assume, there is always something peculiar in its construction—which distinguishes it from an ordinary Tamil sentence. Tamil proverbs have mostly a grammar of their own. Their grammar is chiefly poetic, though often it is also colloquial. The subject and predicate are frequently transposed, case-endings and other particles omitted. There are proverbs in which the subject or predicate is understood. Even corruptions are admissible. It will sometimes be very difficult to make out the case of a noun, especially when there are two or more in the same saying. The passive voice is conspicuous by its absence. It is quite repugnant to the genius of the language. Occasionalḷy even rare words will be met with. To foreigners, therefore, the study of this literature will prove an excellent aid in mastering the principles of colloquial grammar, which is after all the grammar of nine-tenths of the people. As regards antiquity, Tamil proverbs may be divided into three classes, viz. , ancient, middle-aged and modern. Ancient proverbs consist entirely of pure Tamil words without any mixture of Sanskrit. These make up a large proportion, and embrace, for the most part, the opinions, ethics, and customs of the ancient Tamil people. Some of them are so very ancient that some of the words employed are now obsolete. In these no trace of Brahmanical influence can be found. It must be remembered that the Tamil people are converts to Brahmanism, or rather Hinduism as it is now called. Proverbs which have come into use after this conversion belong to the middle ages, and, as may be expected, contain a large number of Sanskrit words. These, however, are not more than a few hundred. A careful study of them will show that the popular verdict is not quite in favour of the Aryan cult. Modern proverbs are still fewer. They relate chiefly to political and agricultural subjects. Some famous Mussulmans and Europeans have been the occasion of a few sayings which by the way reflect little or no credit on them. An enquiry into the teaching of these proverbs ought to find a place here. Taken all in all, this branch of Tamil literature may be called an encyclopædia of Tamil wisdom. They deal with almost every conceivable subject under the sun. Nothing worthy of note seems to have escaped the insight or scrutiny of the Tamil observer. God and man, beast and bird, trees and plants, morality as it affects every condition of life and society, the various departments of human industry and activity, domestic and social relationships, the spheres of hygiene and economy, manners and customs, common sense and wordly wisdom, human follies and vices, and others too numerous to mention, have become the origin of many a pithy proverb. On the all-important subject of morality, their message is as noble as it is wide, as lofty as it is deep. The realm of motives has not been left unexplored by the wise among the Tamil people. The second table in the decalogue has been fully anticipated. As regards positive virtues, they speak in no uncertain tone. 'Where there is love, even the impossible becomes possible.' 'The meek shall rule the earth.' 'Benevolence has ruined none in the world.' 'There is no heaven to those who are merciless.' 'If you want heavenly bliss, give up sensual pleasure.' 'Waste not even a moment.' 'Greatness is always humble.' 'The industrious will never be disgraced.' 'A tree shelters him who fells it.' 'Virtue is its own reward.' 'Silence is worth a thousand.' 'Though it be ambrosia , share it with a guest.' 'Is a flower to be squeezed and smelt?' 'The tears of the poor are like a sharp-edged sword.' These are only a few picked up at random. But what have these proverbs to say about God? Very little indeed. There are more sayings on demons than the Deity. While it is strange that they say so little about their Maker, it must be said to the credit of the Tamils that they have not speculated, like their Aryan proselytizers, on a subject about which they could know or learn little or nothing. The fact that the Tamil word Kadavul (God) does not once occur in the whole range of this literature proves its comparatively recent origin. In the few proverbs which antiquity has bequeathed to us, the term for God is Aiyan ; as in Aiyan alanta padi , 'as God has decreed;' çâkku pôkku çellatu Aiyan mun , 'no excuses will avail with God'; Aiyan amaippai ârâlum talla küdatu . 'no one can violate God's order.' The other sayings in which a Sanskrit term, Teyvam , is employed, belong to the middle period. Aiyan , then, is the ancient Tamil term for God. It is derived from Ai , 'father,' an being the masculine termination. Thus God was the Father, par excellence , to the Tamil people. Their theology was of the simplest kind. They believed in a moral Governor of the Universe, whose will was law, whose decrees were irrevokable and whom they called their Father—a fact over which Professor Max Muller would have rejoiced with all his heart.* Compare the following: 'He is present before we think (of him) and grants what we desire.' God is also called Talaivan , the Chief One, and Munnavan , the first One, as in Tannai ârintavan Talaivanai arivân , 'he who knows There are indeed a few sayings of the middle period in which Aiyanar is used as a term for an inferior god. himself will know God '; and Munnavanê mun nintal mudiyâta porul undô , ' if God be with us, what is impossible ?' Next to theology comes ethics. Like the former, the latter was exceedingly simple. There is no reference in the ancient proverbs to Vedas or Shastras. The light of conscience seems to have been their only guide. It would have been well if these people had been left to their simple beliefs and practices. Conscience they call nenju . Nenjariya poy collalama , 'Can you lie against your conscience ?' Kuttamulla nenju kuru kuru ennum , 'a guilty conscience cannot keep quiet.' But it was very difficult for them to follow this good monitor within. There are many sayings which refer to this universal weakness. 'If you speak the truth, you become an enemy of the village.' 'Seek the approval of your conscience, not that of the village.' 'Even in a healed sore, there will be some matter left.' 'Conscience makes cowards of us all.' 'Fear guilt.' 'Rather die than lose your honour.' It is no wonder that in later days when earnest and truth-seeking Tamil poets came to think for themselves and found no proper remedy for sin, they sang in the way they did and declaimed against the empty ceremonialism and idolatrous practices of their countrymen. Regarding the wisdom and general good sense of the Tamilians their proverbs afford abundant proof. The results of their ripe experience and careful observation they have embodied in sayings which have seldom been surpassed for their beauty or force—not to speak of the rare truths they convey. Here are a few. 'Though the rain has stopped, the tree rain has not.' 'You can stop a boiling pot, but not the mouth of the village.' 'A king and fire are alike.' 'Desire has no limit.'
